clinicalPearls: Cardiac injury is broadly divided into penetrating trauma (most often gunshot or knife wounds, where the entry site is usually obvious) and nonpenetrating, or blunt cardiac injury (BCI).

BCI most commonly follows motor vehicle collisions (rapid deceleration or chest impact) but can also result from falls, crush and blast injuries, assault, or vigorous contact in sports; significant cardiac injury may occur even when there are no external signs of thoracic trauma.

There is no single sign, symptom, or test that confirms BCI, and clinical, laboratory, and radiographic findings are frequently nonspecific in the setting of major trauma, so a high index of suspicion is essential.

An ECG should be obtained in every patient presenting with chest trauma; abnormalities can resemble those of infarction or pericarditis and include sinus tachycardia, RBBB, heart block, ST-T changes, and atrial or ventricular arrhythmias.
Cardiac troponin is more specific than CK-MB for myocardial damage; a normal troponin combined with a normal ECG at 6-8 hours after chest trauma essentially excludes BCI.

Echocardiography is the most useful modality for detecting the structural and functional sequelae of BCI, including regional wall motion abnormalities, pericardial effusion, valvular dysfunction, and ventricular or septal rupture; the RV, interventricular septum, and LV apex are most commonly involved.

Commotio cordis is ventricular fibrillation triggered by a blunt, often innocent-appearing chest impact in the absence of structural injury, occurring most often in adolescents during sports when the blow lands during the vulnerable phase of repolarization (just before the T-wave peak); survival depends on prompt defibrillation.
Sudden emotional or physical stress, even without direct cardiac trauma, may precipitate a transient catecholamine-mediated cardiomyopathy (takotsubo / apical ballooning syndrome).
Because of its anterior position in the chest, the right ventricle is the most frequently injured chamber in penetrating trauma, followed by the left ventricle; isolated atrial injury is uncommon.
Iatrogenic cardiac perforation can complicate central/intracardiac catheter placement, pacemaker or defibrillator lead insertion, RV endomyocardial biopsy, and intracoronary stent deployment.

Post-cardiac injury syndrome (an inflammatory process resembling the postpericardiotomy syndrome) can develop weeks to months after blunt chest trauma, presenting with pericarditis and/or pericardial effusion.

Survivors of penetrating cardiac injury may present days to weeks later with a new murmur or heart failure from an occult or evolving valvular regurgitation or intracardiac shunt, so trauma patients should be re-examined several weeks after injury.
harrison.pathophysiology: Blunt forces (rapid deceleration, direct chest impact, crush, or blast) and penetrating objects damage the myocardium, valves, coronary arteries, pericardium, and great vessels. Myocardial contusion produces injury pathologically similar to infarction, with necrosis arising either directly or from traumatic coronary laceration, dissection, or thrombosis, predisposing to arrhythmias and conduction block. More severe injury causes free wall rupture (hemopericardium and tamponade) or ventricular septal rupture (intracardiac shunting). Valvular apparatus rupture (most often tricuspid or aortic) causes acute incompetence. Aortic rupture or transection, typically just above the aortic valve or at the ligamentum arteriosum tethering point, is the most common vascular deceleration injury. Commotio cordis represents a purely electrical mechanism: a chest blow during the susceptible repolarization window induces ventricular fibrillation without structural damage.
additionalDifferentials: Acute coronary syndrome / myocardial infarction (traumatic coronary dissection or thrombosis can produce STEMI)
Aortic dissection (traumatic aortic rupture can mimic its presentation)
Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy following emotional or physical trauma
Musculoskeletal chest wall pain from rib or sternal injury
additionalInvestigations: 12-lead ECG in all patients with chest trauma (repeat as needed for evolving conduction disturbance/arrhythmia)
Serial cardiac troponin (I or T); normal serial levels make cardiac injury very unlikely
Transthoracic echocardiography in all suspected BCI and all penetrating chest injuries to assess wall motion, effusion, valves, and shunts
Transesophageal echocardiography when adequate TTE images cannot be obtained
Chest x-ray (mediastinal widening suggests aortic injury)
Cardiac catheterization to confirm a suspected mechanical complication (shunt/valvular lesion)
redFlags: Hemodynamic instability or collapse at presentation (penetrating injury mortality approaches 90% in those in hemodynamic collapse)
New loud murmur with rapidly progressive heart failure (traumatic valvular rupture)
Signs of pericardial tamponade (pericardial rub, distant heart sounds, hypotension)
Mediastinal widening on chest x-ray with upper-extremity hypertension and diminished lower-extremity pulses (aortic rupture)
Sudden collapse during chest impact in an athlete (commotio cordis requiring immediate defibrillation)
Even a small pericardial effusion on echo in a penetrating chest injury (suggests occult cardiac perforation)
harrison.prognosis: Outcome depends on injury mechanism, chambers involved, and clinical condition at presentation. Although myocardial rupture is generally fatal, up to ~40% of patients reach a specialized trauma center alive. In penetrating injury, gunshot wounds carry higher mortality than stab wounds (about 20% of shooting victims survive versus up to ~65% of stabbing victims), partly because ballistic injuries more often involve multiple chambers; multichamber involvement carries a worse prognosis than single-chamber injury, and RV injury may carry a better prognosis than LV injury. Patients in hemodynamic collapse on arrival have a mortality near 90%, whereas roughly 75% of those stable enough to reach the operating room survive. Iatrogenic penetrating injuries generally have a better prognosis owing to more limited injury and prompt corrective therapy.
pitfalls: Overlooking cardiac injury because attention is focused on more obvious external injuries.
Relying on sternal or rib fractures to gauge cardiac risk; there is no proven association, and significant cardiac injury can occur with a normal-appearing chest wall.
Using CK-MB to confirm BCI; it is elevated in only ~20% of blunt chest trauma and is falsely raised by massive skeletal muscle injury.
Attributing post-traumatic chest pain solely to musculoskeletal causes when it may reflect myocardial ischemia or pericardial injury.
Assuming a hemodynamically stable penetrating chest injury excludes cardiac involvement; up to ~20% harbor occult cardiac trauma.
Missing delayed complications (post-cardiac injury syndrome, late valvular regurgitation, intracardiac shunt) by not re-examining the patient weeks after injury.
harrison.severityClassification: Blunt cardiac abnormalities span a spectrum (Table 283-1): ECG changes (sinus tachycardia, RBBB, heart block, ST-T changes, arrhythmias), elevated biomarkers (troponin most specific), focal wall motion abnormality or hematoma (RV free wall, LV apex, septum), valvular insufficiency (most often mitral/tricuspid, occasionally aortic), myocardial rupture (VSD or free wall), coronary artery injury (often LAD, presenting as STEMI), and pericardial effusion/tamponade. Risk stratification: stable patients with a normal ECG and normal serial troponins are low risk; an abnormal ECG and/or elevated troponin with a normal echo warrants telemetry monitoring; mechanical complications and hemodynamic instability constitute the highest-acuity group.
